clinicalPearls: A group 1 pre-capillary pulmonary arterial hypertension defined haemodynamically by a raised mean pulmonary artery pressure with an elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and a normal or low pulmonary artery wedge pressure at right heart catheterisation
Most heritable cases carry a loss-of-function mutation in BMPR2, with incomplete penetrance so that many carriers never develop disease and expression varies within families
Autosomal dominant inheritance with markedly reduced penetrance and female predominance means a negative family history does not exclude a genetic cause
Presents insidiously with exertional breathlessness, fatigue, and later syncope, chest pain, and signs of right heart failure such as a loud pulmonary second sound and raised jugular venous pressure
Genetic counselling and cascade testing should be offered, and asymptomatic relatives may enter surveillance echocardiography programmes
Vasoreactivity testing at catheterisation identifies the small minority who may respond to calcium channel therapy; most require targeted pulmonary vasodilator pathways
Compared with idiopathic disease, heritable BMPR2 cases tend to present younger and with more severe haemodynamics
reference.pathophysiology: Heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension arises when a germline mutation, most commonly a loss-of-function variant in the bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2 (BMPR2) gene, impairs BMP signalling in the pulmonary vasculature and shifts the balance toward proliferation over apoptosis. Penetrance is incomplete, so a second hit from environmental, hormonal, or additional genetic factors is generally required for disease to manifest, which explains the female preponderance and variable family expression. The resulting pulmonary arteriolar remodelling comprises intimal proliferation, medial hypertrophy, adventitial thickening, and plexiform lesions that progressively narrow and obliterate small vessels. Rising pulmonary vascular resistance imposes a chronic pressure load on the right ventricle, which hypertrophies and ultimately dilates and fails, producing the pre-capillary haemodynamic profile seen at catheterisation.
additionalDifferentials: Connective tissue disease-associated PAH (e.g. systemic sclerosis)
Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (group 2)
Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease or hypoxia (group 3)
Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease or capillary haemangiomatosis
additionalInvestigations: Right heart catheterisation to confirm pre-capillary haemodynamics and perform acute vasoreactivity testing
Transthoracic echocardiography to estimate pulmonary pressures and assess right ventricular size and function
Ventilation-perfusion scan to exclude chronic thromboembolic disease
Genetic testing for BMPR2 and related PAH genes with counselling and cascade screening of relatives
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing and six-minute walk distance for functional assessment and prognosis
Pulmonary function tests and high-resolution CT to exclude parenchymal lung disease and veno-occlusive features
redFlags: Syncope or presyncope on exertion, indicating a severely limited and vulnerable circulation
Signs of decompensated right heart failure with hypotension, rising jugular venous pressure, or hepatic congestion
Rapidly progressive breathlessness or a falling exercise tolerance suggesting deteriorating haemodynamics
Development of pulmonary oedema after starting vasodilators, raising suspicion of coexisting veno-occlusive disease
reference.prognosis: The natural history is one of progressive right ventricular failure and premature death, though modern targeted therapy delivered through specialist centres has improved survival and functional status. Heritable BMPR2 disease often behaves more aggressively than idiopathic disease, and lung transplantation remains an option for those who progress despite combination therapy.
pitfalls: Assuming the absence of a family history excludes a genetic cause, given the incomplete penetrance of BMPR2 mutations
Diagnosing PAH on echocardiography alone without confirmatory right heart catheterisation and exclusion of post-capillary causes
Prescribing calcium channel therapy to patients who have not demonstrated true acute vasoreactivity
Overlooking coexisting pulmonary veno-occlusive features, where vasodilators can precipitate pulmonary oedema
Delaying referral to a specialist pulmonary hypertension centre where combination therapy and transplant assessment are available
references: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension
management: Initiate targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy through a specialist centre, using endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors or the guanylate cyclase stimulator, and prostacyclin analogues or receptor agonists, with early combination therapy for higher-risk disease
Reserve high-dose calcium channel blockade for the minority who are acute vasoreactive responders at catheterisation
Provide supportive care with diuretics for right heart failure, supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia, and supervised exercise rehabilitation
Advise against pregnancy given its high risk, with counselling on effective contraception, and recommend vaccination against respiratory pathogens

Undertake risk-stratified surveillance with functional class, six-minute walk distance, echocardiography and biomarkers to escalate therapy, and refer for lung transplantation assessment in advanced disease
Offer genetic counselling with cascade BMPR2 testing of relatives and enrol asymptomatic carriers into surveillance echocardiography programmes
Escalate promptly for syncope, progressive right heart failure or clinical deterioration, which signal advanced disease
